html:
The Pawnee, who call themselves Pâri, are a Caddoan-speaking people of the central Great Plains, along the Platte, Loup and Republican rivers in today's Nebraska and Kansas. Their language is related to those of the Wichita, the Arikara and the Caddo further south.

They lived in villages of large, round earth lodges, farmed maize, beans and squash in the river valleys and went out on the plains twice a year to hunt bison. Their religion was tied to the stars; the Skidi band was known for the Morning Star ceremony, which sometimes ended in the sacrifice of a captive girl.

In the 1800s smallpox and attacks by the Lakota wore them down. Many Pawnee men served as scouts for the US Army against the Lakota and Cheyenne. In 1874 and 1875 the Pawnee gave up their Nebraska land and moved to Indian Territory, where the Pawnee Nation of Oklahoma is today. See also the map's other Pawnee territory.
